parts.partTitle: Why Thread Pools Beat Raw Threads

beats.headline: Stop spawning threads manually.
beats.subline: Every new Thread() eats 1MB of stack memory. Here is how to stop crashing your JVM.
beats.narration: Spawning raw threads for every task is a recipe for an OutOfMemoryError. You are burning native memory and killing performance with context switching. The Executor framework is the professional alternative.

beats.title: Executor Lifecycle
beats.subtitle: Decoupling task submission from execution
beats.narration: The ExecutorService acts as a buffer. You submit tasks, and a managed pool of worker threads picks them up. This reuses memory and keeps your service stable under heavy load.

beats.title: The Core Interface Hierarchy

steps.explanation: The base interface for fire-and-forget tasks.
Adds lifecycle control and result-bearing tasks.

beats.narration: Executor is the bare-bones interface for fire-and-forget. Extend it to ExecutorService, and you get lifecycle management like shutdown and the ability to return results via Futures.

beats.title: Raw vs Managed
beats.narration: Raw threads are dangerous. Managed pools provide backpressure and prevent your JVM from hitting the native thread limit. Always prefer the ExecutorService pattern.

beats.title: Part 1 Locked In
beats.nextPartTeaser: Up Next: The hidden traps of ThreadPoolExecutor →
beats.narration: That is the foundation. In Part 2, we dissect the ThreadPoolExecutor algorithm, because the default queue behavior might surprise you.

beats.headline: Does your pool actually grow?
beats.subline: Most developers misunderstand the ThreadPoolExecutor admission algorithm.
beats.narration: Think your pool scales to maximumPoolSize immediately? Think again. The internal algorithm is surprisingly strict, and it is easy to accidentally ignore your max limit entirely.

beats.title: Task Admission Flow
beats.subtitle: The strict 4-step execution logic
beats.narration: First, we spawn core threads. Second, we fill the queue. Only when the queue is full do we spawn burst threads. If everything is full, we trigger the rejection handler.

beats.title: Configuring a Production Pool

steps.explanation: Core vs Max threads define your burst capacity.
Bounded queue is mandatory to force max scaling.

beats.narration: Always use a bounded queue. If you use an unbounded queue, the pool will never spawn burst threads, effectively ignoring your maxPoolSize and risking heap exhaustion.

beats.title: Inspecting Threads
beats.caption: Avoid generic pool names
beats.narration: Use a custom ThreadFactory to name your threads. During an incident, seeing payment-worker-1 is infinitely better than pool-3-thread-14.

beats.title: Part 2 Locked In
beats.nextPartTeaser: Up Next: Callable, Future, and the silent exception trap →
beats.narration: That is the admission logic. In Part 3, we look at Callables and the silent failure trap that makes debugging asynchronous code a nightmare.

beats.headline: Where do your exceptions go?
beats.subline: If you ignore a Future, you ignore the error.
beats.narration: When a Callable throws an exception, it is captured by the Future. If you never call get(), that error vanishes into the void. No logs, no stack trace, just silence.

beats.title: Safe Future Handling

steps.explanation: Captures the result or the exception.
Always use a timeout to prevent deadlocks.
Must unwrap to find the real cause.

beats.narration: Always use timed gets. If the task fails, the exception is wrapped in an ExecutionException. You must call getCause to see what actually went wrong.

beats.title: Task Cancellation
beats.narration: Use cancel(true) to interrupt the worker. But remember, it is cooperative. If your code does not check for interrupts, the thread will keep running.

beats.title: Batch Operations
beats.subtitle: When to use invokeAll vs invokeAny
beats.narration: Need results from multiple sources? invokeAll waits for the group. Need the fastest response from replicas? invokeAny takes the first success and cancels the rest.

beats.title: Part 3 Locked In
beats.nextPartTeaser: Up Next: Sizing pools and the Virtual Thread revolution →
beats.narration: That is the async workflow. In Part 4, we cover sizing math and why Java 21 Virtual Threads change everything.

beats.headline: Stop guessing your pool size.
beats.subline: Use math, not intuition, to size your thread pools.
beats.narration: Sizing pools is not about picking a random number like 200. It is about the ratio of wait time to compute time. And with Virtual Threads, the old rules are changing fast.

beats.title: The Sizing Formula
beats.subtitle: Threads = Cores * Util * (1 + Wait/Compute)
beats.narration: For CPU tasks, keep it close to your core count. For I/O, use the wait-to-compute ratio. But on Java 21, just use Virtual Threads for I/O and forget the pool math.

beats.title: Java 21 Virtual Threads
beats.narration: Virtual threads are not pooled. They are created per task and garbage collected. This is the new standard for blocking I/O workloads in modern Java.

beats.title: Graceful Shutdown
beats.caption: The two-phase shutdown pattern
beats.narration: Never just kill your process. Use the two-phase shutdown: stop accepting new tasks, wait for existing ones, and force-stop only if the timeout hits.

beats.title: Chapter Complete
beats.narration: You have mastered thread pools. Checkout the companion branch to run the labs yourself. See you in the next level.
